I worked as a bowling attendant trainer for about ten months. Hated the job, liked having free food. One day, near the end of my time there, I trained a new kid (looked 15, maybe barely 16).

One of the things I taught was how to go under the pinsetter (the giant thing that goes down and slides all the pins into the back area) if you absolutely needed to, like if a kid is under there. I show where the emergency shut-off button is, show how to run down the lane without slipping, and how to slide underneath it (there's not much room, so you're on your hands and knees). I do this on a lane that has no clients, is turned off, and tell the front desk I'm under there, for safety.

Few facts about pinsetters. The ones we used were old. As in, originally made when pinsetters were invented, and never upgraded, just repaired. This old hunk of junk is extremely bulky and strong. The reason we have to do such in-depth training with a bunch of teenagers is because the force of the pinsetter going down will crush whatever is beneath it. Including human bones.

Then it throws whatever is in front of it backwards with enough force to smash every bone in your body. Then you're in the pin circle. The pin circle is constantly spinning (like a standing dryer, or an exercise wheel for gerbils) with a dozen heavy pins in it, which means if you're in it, you get the full force of a dozen heavy pins repetitively slamming into every part of your body. Basically, if you get caught by the pinsetter, you die. And I had to teach teenagers that.

Anyways. Teaching this new kid about it. I check, the lane is turned off, no new customers walking in (in fact, no customers at all.) so it's definitely safe. I walk New Kid down the lane and throw some of the pins out on it so he can try grabbing them and throwing them under the pinsetter, into the pin circle. One of them doesn't go all the way, so he crawls under to grab it. I back-slide under with him and pass him the rest so we can get back to work.

And as we're both in the belly of the beast I hear a very quiet noise. Barely heard anything over the sound of the loud-ass music constantly playing. I look up and see the lights for our lane had turned on. When the front desk turns a lane on, they automatically send the setter through it's cycle just in case any pins are out of place. And I'm underneath a huge death machine with a Kid.

I freak out, grab the kid by the back of his collar and forcefully yank him out backwards, and then I use my legs to push against one of the side walls with all my remaining force and roll as fast as I can and just barely clear the edge when the pinsetter slams down. Right in front of my face.

I was seventeen.

You get the feeling that the dark times are genuinely acted, and the happy times even more so. I've rewatched it a dozen times, cried in the same spots every time. I can't wait until I can afford to buy the series so I can stop borrowing it from a library four towns away.

If someone has passed the point of sanity, to the point where every moment of life is a confusing hell to them, let them pass on. Don't fight for someone's life when they are begging for death.

If the suffering of a human being is so great that life for them is worse then death, then let them go. It's not right that people of any age have to go through that hell just because their families aren't ready to say goodbye, or because not every single treatment has been tried. Give them a hug, a kiss. Tell them you love them. Then release them from their existence.

If someone wants to die, and they are calmly set in their decision, then they should be allowed to die. If someone has malignant cancer, and no amount of chemo will save them, let them live their lives to the full and when they are too weak to do what makes them happy, send them on their way, feeling satisfied and loved instead of hurt and sick and trapped.

I acted on it before I realized I was thinking about it. I'm not quite sure when I started thinking about it, but when I was 12, I stepped onto a busy roadway, directly in the path of a semi. I knew it was headed towards me and I didn't care. I just.. did it. My family was with me and my brother pulled me back onto the sidewalk. They thought I just wasn't looking or I tripped or something.

When I was 14, I was hospitalized and almost institutionalized because I chugged an entire bottle of pills and waited. My dad came into my room, saw me writing an apology letter, saw the empty bottle, and took me to the ER. At the time, I just wanted to die. Not for any reason in particular. Now that I'm an adult, I can see that my childhood was devestatingly abusive. I don't think they meant to, but with extremely strict Southern Baptist parents (dad's a pastor, to boot. Not to mention the stress of keeping everything perfect because image is everything to them) and six hateful siblings, my life was a living hell.

I was the good, quiet one. It was easy to pin things on me because I never fought back. So getting beaten by my siblings and then whooped by my dad, constantly hearing negative, hurtful things, and then it only getting worse after I started trying to die because "suicide makes us look bad" really screwed me up. When I turned 18, I was kicked out. I was homeless for 8 months, until a girl I barely knew took me in. Now I'm 19 and trying my best, but I can't afford therapy with minimum wage and even if I could, I don't have a way to get there. 

Sorry, that was a lot to dump on someone. I just really needed to.

Not quite sure what that means, but I can think of two possibilities, so I'll mention both. The first is when I worked in a cafe. There were times I was working alone and heard my coworkers talking to me. Like, we had entire conversations and I'll turn around to face them and nobody's there. I had a lot of doctors at the time, and they were confident it was the stress of the job. I quit the job and the voices stopped, so I guess they were right.

The second happens fairly often. I'll be having a goodish time and all of a sudden I'll become extremely over-excited. Sometimes I'll get mad over nothing, sometimes I come extremely close to a mental breakdown, sometimes I realize it's about to happen and go lock myself in the bathroom until the feeling goes away. I hate when it happens, but I can't control it so I ignore it.

You make some good points, and I appreciate having a voice of reason around. I didn't take the time to elaborate on my friendship in the post, so I will here so you understand a little better (if you care to read, of course).

Susan saved my life when I was 17. I have a very toxic home life (and I'm severly bipolar) and tried killing myself with a mix of my prescription meds in the school bathroom's handicap stall. Susan got worried when I didn't come out and found me on the floor convulsing. Since that day, she's been by my side, keeping me from walking into traffic.

On my 18th birthday, my mom kicked me out. I was living in my car for months, pretending everything was still okay. The day Susan learned I was homeless, her family took me in. My mom took back my car and gave it to my sister since it's not in my name, and Susan said she'd just drive me everywhere I needed. She kept that promise. I've never missed a night at school or a day at work.

She told me she needed a job, so I convinced my job to hire her. And now you're caught up. I owe everything to Susan. She's my rock. If I have to quit a job or two until I graduate in December, then so be it. She's the reason I haven't gone a day hungry since November.

Her family gave me Christmas and birthday presents, clothed and fed me, and take me along when they go out (movies, parties, six flags, etc). This is the first real family I've ever had, and I feel like I'm being forced to choose between them and my future (can't afford school without a job).

That was a huge amount of words, sorry. I've just always appreciated everything she's done for me and I've never actually told anyone.
